author: Buzzy Hassrick, Reporter buzzy@codyenterprise.com
title: Steward: House divided | Local News | codyenterprise.com
text:
For 23 years, Scott Steward has been going to Cheyenne during the legislative session. This time, he came away from his recent visit with a novel impression.
“I’ve never seen this much dissension and infighting in the House,” he said. “It’s divided, it’s very divided, in my opinion. It’s between conservative Republicans and the Freedom Caucus. I have no problem keeping government in check,” but the Freedom Caucus members “seem to be cutting just to cut. The Senate seems to be doing better,” enacting fewer amendments.
Along with his in-person visit, Steward has been watching clips online of the session. “The legislature is always contentions,” he said, “but this year there’s a lot more heat. At times, there a lack of respect for each other.”
His recent trip during the budget session was as the new chair of the Board of Park County Commissioners. He discussed some bills that are supported or opposed by the Wyoming County Commissioners Association.
The WCCA strongly opposed Senate File 0108 that was sponsored by Sen. Dan Laursen of Powell, which would require hand-counting election ballots. WCCA called it an “unfunded mandate.”
For Steward, the cost in time and money was one reason for his opposition. Another reason was the state requirement that results be submitted by 10:30 p.m. on election nights.
“It’d be hard to meet that deadline” with hand-counting, he said.
Still, Steward added, “I’m 100% for checking voting machines and have 100% confidence in them.” Yet “not everyone feels confident, so it’s time to put this to rest and prove it.
“I really feel it’s accurate, but we need to show the public.”
SF108 died in the Senate. Steward said he supported HB0108, which WCCA also endorsed, which sets up a system for selecting four precincts for hand-counts and comparing those results with the machine tally. If those sums differ, he said, the issue would have to be addressed.
A former Park County Sheriff, Steward said he opposes another bill, SF0101, as does every sheriff in every county. It’s called the “Second Amendment Protection Act,” a misleading title, in his opinion, because protections already exist. “It creates something that doesn’t need to be there,” he added. Steward said the proposal likely resulted from ICE incidents, although “local law enforcement can’t enforce federal regulations anyway.”
The bill would prohibit law enforcement officers in the state from participating in federal task forces on joint projects, meaning “DCI (state Department of Criminal Investigation) “would have to pull out of joint operation,” Steward said. It would also prevent Park County Sheriff’s Deputies from serving as special deputies in Yellowstone National Park.
“It’s horrible. It’s a convoluted and badly written law.” he said. “It would prohibit any interaction with the feds. It would hamstring local law enforcement and harm communities.”
Steward cited a local-federal joint operation that went from Big Horn County to California and Washington and sent in 35-40 people to prison on drug charges. Under the proposed bill, a local law enforcement officer who helped the feds would be fined $50,000.
Another bill, HB107, received strong support from WCCA. It deals with the distribution of the state’s use and sales taxes to cities and counties, resulting in a steady stream of revenue to the counties, Steward said. Last year, he noted, Park County lost about $2.7 million because of the 25% cut in residential property taxes.
“I know we’re going to need to cut services,” he added.
Another proposal supported by WCCA, HB0036, is probably a response to the grass fires in the southeastern part of the state last year, Steward said. It would establish two modules of administrative fire-fighting teams at the state level to oversee responses to big wildfires, he said. They may occur here “if we don’t get some moisture,” he added.
“There’s been ¼ inch of snow at my house on the North Fork this year,” Steward said Tuesday, unlike the usual depth in feet. “We’re getting some rain today, and there’s snow up high, but it goes away in a day or so.”
